title: Index Fossils: Nature's Timestamps
objective: After this level you can explain how short-lived, widespread fossils let geologists match rock layers across continents.
summary: William Smith found fossils in the same order everywhere. Index fossils, from short-lived, widespread species, let geologists match rock layers of the same age across the world.

cards.headline: A canal surveyor cracked the code of rock layers with his fossil collection.
cards.body: In the 1790s, William Smith kept finding the same fossils in the same layers of English rock. That hunch let geologists match rocks across whole continents.

cards.headline: Same order, everywhere
cards.body: Smith was a surveyor planning canal routes, so he studied rocks up close. He saw that fossils in sedimentary rock always show up in a set order from bottom to top, and that the same order turns up in rocks elsewhere. That's faunal succession. With it he could identify a layer wherever it was exposed, and in 1815 he published a geologic map of England and Wales. Fossils had become a barcode for rock.

cards.headline: What makes a good timestamp
cards.body: Not every fossil helps. The best index fossils are easy to recognize, abundant, spread over a wide area, and from a species that lasted only a short span of geologic time. Short-lived is the key. If a species existed only briefly, any rock holding it must have formed during that brief window.
cards.callout: Easy to spot, common, widespread, short-lived

cards.fact: Rocks far apart that share an index fossil formed in the same slice of time.
cards.context: Fossils record the slow development of life, so geologists use index fossils to identify rocks of the same age throughout the world, even with oceans in between. Ammonoids, extinct sea animals, are among the favorites.

cards.headline: Index fossils: matched
learned: Fossils appear in the same order everywhere
William Smith mapped England and Wales by fossils
Index fossils are common, widespread and short-lived
Shared index fossils mean the same age

questions.prompt: Which trait lets an index fossil pin down a narrow slice of time?

options.label: It is unusually large
options.rationale: Size doesn't narrow the time window.

options.label: Its species lived for only a short span
It is found in only one small area
It is still alive today
options.rationale: A living species spans too much time.

questions.explanation: A short-lived species means any rock holding it formed during that brief window.

questions.prompt: How can a fossil show that rock layers on two different continents formed at the same time?

options.label: Both layers hold the same short-lived, widespread species
Both layers are the same color and thickness
options.rationale: Similar-looking rock can form at very different times.

options.label: Both layers sit at the same depth underground
options.rationale: Depth varies from place to place.

options.label: Both layers contain some kind of fossil
options.rationale: Only a short-lived, recognizable species narrows the time.

questions.explanation: Rocks that share an index fossil formed while that short-lived species was alive.

questions.prompt: A limestone is packed with shells of a short-lived index species. What does that tell you about the limestone?

options.label: It formed after the species went extinct
options.rationale: The shells had to exist before they could be packed into the rock.

options.label: It must be the oldest rock in the area
options.rationale: Index fossils give a time window, not the oldest rank.

options.label: It started as mud of silt and clay
options.rationale: That's shale; limestone is built from shells.

options.label: It formed while that species was alive

questions.explanation: Limestone is often built from the shells of sea creatures, so it formed while that index species lived.
